content.content:
## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: a field's own popup, the settings panel and the day
preview. Nothing rises from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either
thumb and does not pretend to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**An entry that already exists opens read-only.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day
preview, or as a card on the board — opens a **view popup** that shows it, and a pen in that
popup's top row opens the **edit popup**. Most openings are to read: what day is this on, what is
on the agenda, who is coming. A form answers those questions in input boxes, which are harder to
read than text, and it leaves every value one slip away from being changed by a tap meant to
scroll. A new entry has nothing to read, so the `+` and a click on empty space open the edit
popup directly.

### The view popup

A top row, and then the entry. The row carries **the type as a marker, not a choice** — a ticked
square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and not pressable — and then,
right-aligned, a trashcan to delete the entry, a **pen** to edit it, and an `x` to close:

```
[☑]                          [trash] [pen] [x]
```

The trashcan stays here rather than moving behind the pen. Deleting is not an edit of a field, and
the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two taps depends on the trashcan being
on the first of them.

Below the row: the title, when it is, and then **only the fields that are set**, in the canonical
order the edit popup's rows use. An entry with a title and a date shows a title and a date.
Nothing here is a row waiting to be filled — that is what the pen is for — so an unset field has
nothing to say and is left out, which also means the set-first ordering below is simply the
canonical order here.

**The details body is shown in full and rendered**, not clipped to two lines and not as raw
markdown, by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card and
the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing.

**A repeating entry says so**, and carries its `skip this one`: skipping drops a single
occurrence, which is an action on the entry like deleting it, not a change to a field. The scope
pair is not here — it governs what an edit writes, and in a popup that writes nothing it would
read as a choice about what you are looking at.

### The edit popup

A row of icon buttons at the top, and it holds the type pair and the three on the right and
nothing between them. **Every button in it is an icon; no button carries a letter.**

- Leftmost, a ticked square for **task** and a calendar page for **event**. Choosing one
  deselects the other; the default is event. What the entry *is* comes first, because it governs
  what the rest of the popup offers. **On an entry that already exists the pair is disabled** —
  it shows which of the two this is and refuses to change it. A task turned into an event drops
  its stage, its importance and its estimate, and a popup opened to fix a typo is not where that
  belongs one tap away. The type is settled when the entry is made.
- Then, right-aligned: a trashcan to delete the entry, a disk to save it, and an `x` to close and
  discard. **The `x` is rightmost, in every popup in Mine.** The way out of an overlay sits in the
  same corner wherever you are, so leaving one is never something to look for — and that corner
  is worth more to the button you reach for by habit than to the one you aim at. The disk gives
  it up and sits beside it.

There is no dash between the two groups: the gap to the right-aligned trio already separates
them, and the field icons the dash used to divide off are not in this row at all any more.

Below it, in this order: the **title**, the **start and end** fields, the **toggle row**, and
then **one row per field**.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under start and end. These are not fields with a form each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself, and they **show their value** rather than merely whether
they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one that opens a popup, because a number has to be typed.
  Its badge reads the day count as `2d`. It stays on this row rather than joining the field rows
  below, because what it carries is a badge-sized value like the other three, not a form.

On an event, stage, important and estimate are not there at all, because an event has none of
them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is the save button's green: in all of Mine green is a save
and red is a trashcan, and a green toggle beside the disk would make the popup look like it
offers two primary actions.

### The field rows

Every other field is a row, and **every field has a row, set or not** — the rows are now the only
way to reach a field, so none of them can be hidden. A row is the icon on the left and the
field's name beside it, and, when the field is set, its value after that:

```
[ball]    Category     Work
[pin]     Location     Conference room 3B
[lines]   Details
[repeat]  Repeat
```

The six fields, in their canonical order:

- three lines of text for **details** — the markdown body;
- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

- **Clicking a row opens that field's popup.** The row *is* the pen, so no row carries one, and
  clearing a field is the trashcan inside its popup, which is already there.
- **The rows that are set move to the top.** Set fields come first, unset ones follow, and inside
  each group the order is always the canonical one above. Setting a field lifts its row into the
  top group and shuffles nothing else, so a row never moves for a reason you did not cause.
- **A set row is plain.** Being in the top group and showing a value is what says the field is
  set — which is what the old lit icon said, in a row that no longer exists. Nothing in the
  popup lights except the two toggles on the row above, `24h` and `!`.

Each of the six opens its own popup, and every popup has the same three buttons in the entry
popup's own order: a trashcan that clears that one field, a disk that commits the value into the
entry form, and, rightmost, an `x` that abandons the sub-edit. **A sub-popup never writes to the
repo**, now with no exception at all: a group is added in settings, not from an entry.
Nothing is written until the entry popup's own disk, so one entry edit is one commit, and the
entry popup's `x` discards the staged fields along with everything else. This is also what makes
a brand-new entry work, since it has no file for a sub-popup to write to.

Saving **closes the popup and returns to the calendar immediately**; the push to GitHub runs in
the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the popup. **Both ways out land on the
calendar**, the disk and the `x` alike, even when the edit was reached by the pen from a view
popup. Stepping back to the preview would leave a popup open over a change already committed, and
the cell or the card behind it shows the result anyway.

### Discarding an edit

**Leaving a popup that holds unsaved changes asks first.** The `x`, a click on the backdrop and

read as a choice about what you are looking at.

### The edit popup

A row of icon buttons at the top, and it holds the type pair and the three on the right and
nothing between them. **Every button in it is an icon; no button carries a letter.**

- Leftmost, a ticked square for **task** and a calendar page for **event**. Choosing one
  deselects the other; the default is event. What the entry *is* comes first, because it governs
  what the rest of the popup offers. **On an entry that already exists the pair is disabled** —
  it shows which of the two this is and refuses to change it. A task turned into an event drops
  its stage, its importance and its estimate, and a popup opened to fix a typo is not where that
  belongs one tap away. The type is settled when the entry is made.
- Then, right-aligned: a trashcan to delete the entry, a disk to save it, and an `x` to close and
  discard. **The `x` is rightmost, in every popup in Mine.** The way out of an overlay sits in the
  same corner wherever you are, so leaving one is never something to look for — and that corner
  is worth more to the button you reach for by habit than to the one you aim at. The disk gives
  it up and sits beside it.

There is no dash between the two groups: the gap to the right-aligned trio already separates
them, and the field icons the dash used to divide off are not in this row at all any more.

Below it, in this order: the **title**, the **start and end** fields, the **toggle row**, and
then **one row per field**.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under start and end. These are not fields with a form each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself, and they **show their value** rather than merely whether
they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one that opens a popup, because a number has to be typed.
  Its badge reads the day count as `2d`. It stays on this row rather than joining the field rows
  below, because what it carries is a badge-sized value like the other three, not a form.

On an event, stage, important and estimate are not there at all, because an event has none of
them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is the save button's green: in all of Mine green is a save
and red is a trashcan, and a green toggle beside the disk would make the popup look like it
offers two primary actions.

### The field rows

Every other field is a row, and **every field has a row, set or not** — the rows are now the only
way to reach a field, so none of them can be hidden. A row is the icon on the left and the
field's name beside it, and, when the field is set, its value after that:

```
[ball]    Category     Work
[pin]     Location     Conference room 3B
[lines]   Details
[repeat]  Repeat
```

The six fields, in their canonical order:

- three lines of text for **details** — the markdown body;
- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

- **Clicking a row opens that field's popup.** The row *is* the pen, so no row carries one, and
  clearing a field is the trashcan inside its popup, which is already there.
- **The rows that are set move to the top.** Set fields come first, unset ones follow, and inside
  each group the order is always the canonical one above. Setting a field lifts its row into the
  top group and shuffles nothing else, so a row never moves for a reason you did not cause.
- **A set row is plain.** Being in the top group and showing a value is what says the field is
  set — which is what the old lit icon said, in a row that no longer exists. Nothing in the
  popup lights except the two toggles on the row above, `24h` and `!`.

Each of the six opens its own popup, and every popup has the same three buttons in the entry
popup's own order: a trashcan that clears that one field, a disk that commits the value into the
entry form, and, rightmost, an `x` that abandons the sub-edit. **A sub-popup never writes to the
repo**, now with no exception at all: a group is added in settings, not from an entry.
Nothing is written until the entry popup's own disk, so one entry edit is one commit, and the
entry popup's `x` discards the staged fields along with everything else. This is also what makes
a brand-new entry work, since it has no file for a sub-popup to write to.

Saving **closes the popup and returns to the calendar immediately**; the push to GitHub runs in
the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the popup. **Both ways out land on the
calendar**, the disk and the `x` alike, even when the edit was reached by the pen from a view
popup. Stepping back to the preview would leave a popup open over a change already committed, and
the cell or the card behind it shows the result anyway.

questions.question: How does creating an entry work, now that every row writes straight to the file? (`+` and a click on empty space currently open the edit popup with a draft, and the title is required.)

options.label: Title first, then it exists (Recommended)
options.description: A new entry opens the same popup with the **title row already active** and the when-row seeded from where you created it. Saving the title creates the file; from then on every row writes through like any other entry. The other rows are inert until it exists, so there is one popup and one rule, and abandoning a `+` writes nothing.

## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: the hamburger panel and the day preview. Nothing rises
from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend
to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**There is one popup, and it is both.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day preview, or
as a card on the board — opens the entry, shown as text, and **every value in it is edited where
it is read**: click the thing, change it, save it. There is no pen, no second popup behind one,
and no mode to be in.

It was two before, a read-only preview with a pen into a form, and the reason was sound: a form
answers *what day is this on* in input boxes, which are harder to read than text and leave every
value one slip away from a tap meant to scroll. Editing in place keeps that — a row is text until
it is clicked, so there is still nothing to slip into — and gives back the two things the split
cost. A change was four taps: open, pen, field, save. And the preview and the form had to agree
about every field twice over, in two blocks of code, which is how one of them came to show the
stage and the other to hide it.

**Each row saves itself, and a save reaches the repo.** There is no disk in the top row, because
there is no draft to commit: the row's own save writes the file and queues the push, and the sync
line reports it as it reports every other write. One entry edited in four fields is therefore up
to four commits where it used to be one — the price of the popup always showing what is actually
stored, and a fair one against a history whose job is to be readable.

```
[☑]                                  [trash] [x]      an entry that exists
[☑] [📅]                                       [x]    a new one: the type is still a choice
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry and an `x` to
close. On an entry that already exists the type is a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square
for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and not pressable — because a task turned into an
event drops its stage, its importance and its estimate, and the type is settled when the entry is
made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the event selected.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group rather than beside the `x`: deleting is not an edit
of a field, and the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two taps depends on the
trashcan being on the first of them.

Below the row, in this order: the **title**, the **scope and skip** row on a repeating entry, the
**when**, the **toggle row**, **one row per field**, and the **details body** last.

### A row, and a row being edited

Every row is **the icon, then the value** — no field name beside it:

```
[ball]    Work                                      [trash]
[pin]     Conference room 3B                        [trash]
[repeat]  Repeat
[bell]    Alerts
```

The name is gone because it said the same thing as the icon it sat beside, in the one column
where the value has to fit. **An unset row shows the field's name in its place, muted** — which
is what an empty input does everywhere else in Mine, and what keeps a bell from being a bell and
nothing else. A set row reads as a value; an unset one reads as an invitation.

- **The rows that are set move to the top.** Set fields come first, unset ones follow, and inside
  each group the order is always the canonical one below. Setting a field lifts its row into the
  top group and shuffles nothing else, so a row never moves for a reason you did not cause.
- **A set row carries a trashcan at its right**, which clears that field and writes at once. An
  unset row has nothing to clear and carries none. There is no prompt: a cleared field is typed
  again, which is not what a deleted entry is.
- **Clicking a row makes it active.** The value becomes the control for it, in the row itself, and
  the row's right-hand end becomes **trashcan, save, `x`** — the same three in the same order as
  every popup in Mine, which is where that field's own popup used to put them. The save writes;
  the `x` abandons what was typed; the trashcan clears the field.
- **Only one row is active at a time.** Clicking another row while one is active is the same as
  that row's `x`, and asks the same question if there is something to lose.
- **Clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row.** This is the rule a kanban card already
  holds to, and it matters more here, because the trashcan now sits on the surface being tapped.
  The row and its controls are one place where a click that does two things is easy to build.

The six fields, in their canonical order:

- three lines of text for **details** — the markdown body;
- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

**Every editor opens in its own row.** There is no popup over the popup any more: the field

### Repetition

A dropdown, not an RRULE field:

```
does not repeat · daily · weekly · every 2 weeks ·
monthly on the x-th · monthly on the x-th weekday · yearly
```

below it an **ends** control: never, on a date, or after a number of occurrences.

Files may be hand-written or imported, so a rule the dropdown cannot express — `the last Friday
of the month`, `Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays` — is shown as a non-selectable **custom** state
displaying the rule as text, with a note that choosing an option will replace it. Saving the
entry without touching the dropdown leaves the rule untouched. No hand-written rule is ever
silently rewritten.

### Category

**One list, two forms.** It is the same list of groups wherever it is opened, each with its
colour — but what it lets you do depends on where you came from, and the two sets of controls
never appear together.

- **Reached from an entry it only picks.** The groups and nothing else: no pen, no trashcan, no
  `+ add category`. Naming, recolouring and deleting a group are settings, and an entry popup is
  not where a list the whole repo shares should be rewritten — least of all by a trashcan a
  thumb's width from the group being aimed at. The way to clear the field is the popup's own
  trashcan, as in the other five, so there is no `no category` row in the list either: that was a
  second way to do what the trio at the top already does, and the trio is the one that sits in
  the same place in every field's popup.
- **Reached from the settings panel's *edit groups* it only manages.** Every group with its
  colour, a pen, a trashcan and a `+ add`, and no way to pick one, because nothing is being
  filled in. Adding a group asks for a label and a colour; its stored name is derived from the
  label and never shown, which is why relabelling or recolouring later touches no entry. Entries
  still naming a deleted group render grey.

This is **the only place in the calendar where a group is named or coloured**. One list, because
two would have to be kept in step and neither would gain anything by it.

Because adding a group now sits behind the gear, **nothing in a field's popup reaches the repo at
all** and the rule above has no exception left to carve out. `groups.md` is written the moment the
settings list commits a change — a different file from any entry, and nothing an entry popup is
holding unsaved.

a day header in the week grid. The day view has no header to reach it from, and needs none: it
is already showing the one day the preview would list.

## Rendering a range

1. Collect dated entries whose `start` falls in the range.
2. Expand every rule in `recurring/` over the range; drop dates in `exdate`, add `rdate`.
3. Replace an occurrence with the override matching `series` + `recurrence-id`; an override
   marked cancelled removes it.
4. Drop groups switched off in the filter.
5. Sort: all-day first, then by start time.

Index overrides by `` `${series}|${recurrenceId}` `` once per load; a linear scan per occurrence
is what makes month views slow.

p='calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md'
s=open(p).read()
a="## Modules\n"
b="""## Writes from the popup

One row's save is one write. The title's first save on a new entry is `createEntry`; every save
after that is `updateEntry`, or `saveOverride` when the scope pair says `this occurrence`. The
popup stays open, so this is the first place in the app that writes the same entry repeatedly
from one screen, and three things follow that the save-once-and-close popup never had to handle.

**The popup re-points at the saved entry after every write.** `S.reload()` rebuilds the model, so
the occurrence object the popup was opened with is stale the moment a row saves: its `data` is a
generation behind and its `baseOid` with it. The popup must take the reloaded occurrence and draw
from that. Holding the old object is the bug this note exists for, and it does not look like one
— the row shows the right value, because the row put it there, and only the *next* row's save
goes out with a stale base and lands as a conflict against a file the user themselves just wrote.

**A date change moves the file.** The day is in the path and the API has no rename, so the when
row's save is a delete plus a create — and the popup must then follow the entry to its new path,
for the same reason. A popup still pointing at the old path writes a file that no longer exists.

**A drain collapses queued writes per path.** Several saves can queue before a drain — offline,
or faster than the chain runs — and `POST /git/trees` is handed one entry per queued item, so the
same path would appear more than once in a single tree. The drain keeps the **last** text for a
path and drops the earlier entries. The `baseOid` needs no choosing: `putFile` leaves the local
`oid` alone on a queued write, so every queued put for a path already carries the same base, which
is the one the first edit was made against and the right one to detect a real conflict with.

**Nothing writes before the entry exists.** On a new entry the rows other than the title are
inert — not merely ignored on click, but drawn as such — because there is no file to patch and no
path to patch it at. The title's save is what creates both.

## Modules
"""
assert a in s; s=s.replace(a,b,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PYEOF

+from one screen, and three things follow that the save-once-and-close popup never had to handle.
+**The popup re-points at the saved entry after every write.** `S.reload()` rebuilds the model, so
+the occurrence object the popup was opened with is stale the moment a row saves: its `data` is a
+generation behind and its `baseOid` with it. The popup must take the reloaded occurrence and draw
+from that. Holding the old object is the bug this note exists for, and it does not look like one
+— the row shows the right value, because the row put it there, and only the *next* row's save
+goes out with a stale base and lands as a conflict against a file the user themselves just wrote.
+**A date change moves the file.** The day is in the path and the API has no rename, so the when
+row's save is a delete plus a create — and the popup must then follow the entry to its new path,
+for the same reason. A popup still pointing at the old path writes a file that no longer exists.
+**A drain collapses queued writes per path.** Several saves can queue before a drain — offline,
+or faster than the chain runs — and `POST /git/trees` is handed one entry per queued item, so the
+same path would appear more than once in a single tree. The drain keeps the **last** text for a
+path and drops the earlier entries. The `baseOid` needs no choosing: `putFile` leaves the local
+`oid` alone on a queued write, so every queued put for a path already carries the same base, which
+is the one the first edit was made against and the right one to detect a real conflict with.
+**Nothing writes before the entry exists.** On a new entry the rows other than the title are
+inert — not merely ignored on click, but drawn as such — because there is no file to patch and no
+path to patch it at. The title's save is what creates both.

narrow phone on its own.

**An existing entry opens read-only.** That clicking one — in a grid, in the day preview and as a
card on the board alike — opens a popup containing **no input, select or textarea at all**, and
that its top row runs trashcan, pen, `x` with no disk in it. That the type is shown as something
not pressable. That **only the fields that are set appear**: an entry with a title and a date
renders no location row and no alerts row, which is the check that stops the preview quietly
becoming the form again. That the pen opens the edit popup, and that a `+` or a click on empty
space opens the edit popup directly with no preview in between.

**The shared renderer, where the preview uses it.** That a details body holding `## Agenda`, a
`- ` bullet, a `- [x]` and a `- [ ]`, `**bold**` and a link renders as a heading element, a list
with a ticked and an unticked box, a bold element and an anchor whose href is the link's — and
that a `javascript:` URL in the same body produces no anchor at all. That a body containing
`<script>alert(1)</script>` puts that text on the screen and adds **no script element to the
document**: the renderer builds nodes and never markup, and this is the check that keeps it so.
That a ticked checkbox in the preview is not pressable.

**The entry popup's icon row, toggle row and field rows.** That the edit popup's icon row holds
icons alone, with no letter anywhere in it, and that it holds nothing but the type pair and the
three on the right — task, event, then delete, save, close — with no field icon and no dash left
in it. That **the type pair is disabled on an entry that already exists** and enabled on a new
one, resolved from the buttons' disabled state and not from how they look.

**That the `x` is the rightmost control in every popup**: the entry popup, each of the six field
sub-popups, the day preview and the hamburger panel. Resolved from the buttons' left edges, so a
row that reads correctly but was built in the old order cannot pass — and a check that only
counted three buttons would have passed on the old order, which is why this one reads their
positions. That the entry popup's and a sub-popup's trio runs trashcan, save, `x` in that order.

That a new entry is an event and its toggle row holds `24h` by itself; that choosing a task puts
stage, important and estimate on that same row and switching back to an event takes all three
away again. That stage cycles through three stages in three badge colours and back; that
**important is a toggle and not a cycle** — two taps return it to where it started, it carries no
badge and no digit, and there is no third state to reach; and that the estimate opens a popup
prefilled with one day, badges `3d` once set and loses its badge once cleared. That `24h` and `!`
light with the ordinary enabled background and never with `--good`, because green is the save
button's, and that nothing else in the popup lights at all. That the row sits **below** the start
and end fields, not above them — resolved from the elements' document order, since a row that
merely looks right can still be the old one.

That the six field rows read details, category, repeat, alerts, location, participants, in that
order on a task and on an event alike, each one carrying its icon and its name; that every field
has a row whether it is set or not; that setting one moves its row above the unset ones while the
order inside each group stays canonical; that a set row shows the field's value and no pen; and
that a set row carries no enabled background, because position and value are what say it is set.

**A repeating entry, which the fixture now carries.** Nothing in it repeated before, so the
scope pair, the skip and the override paths had no entry to run against at all. That the preview
says the entry repeats and carries `skip this one`, and that the **scope pair is not on it**.
That switching scope and then leaving **asks nothing**: switching rebuilds the draft from the
other file, so it has to rebuild the baseline a discard is measured against too — a baseline left
behind reads as undefined, which makes every way out of the popup ask about changes nobody made.

content.content:
Almost everything that has actually broken here is a layout or a wiring fault — a grid track
that will not shrink, a button that stops being wired when its markup moves, a key written into
the frontmatter that should have been left out. None of those show up in a function test, which
is why the bulk of the checks drive the real app.

The exception is the model arithmetic — dates, ISO weeks, sprints, recurrence expansion, the
zone conversion, and what a write actually serialises. It is pure: `calendar/data.js` imports
nothing that needs a DOM, and `buildModel` takes files rather than reading them. A date bug there
surfaces in the browser as a cell in the wrong place, a minute into the run, which is the worst
possible instrument for it. So `test/unit.mjs` calls those functions directly and runs first.

## How the harness works

`test/unit.mjs` is plain node — no framework, no dependencies, same one-line-per-check output.
=== 348-360 ===
Headless Chromium on a desktop is not a phone. It does not cover:

- **the real device** — a system font scale, a notch, a software keyboard, Safari's and
  Chrome's own quirks. Serve the tree with `python3 -m http.server` and open it from the phone
  on the same network, or push and open the live URL.
- **installing to the home screen, the service worker and the update banner** — these need an
  installed app over HTTPS. `spike/` covers the platform questions and needs no token.
- **GitHub sync**: pulling, the one-commit drain, conflict files, an expiring token. Only a real
  token against the real data repo exercises those, and that is done by hand.

A change to any of those three is checked on a device before it ships, and
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) records what was found and when.

# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries,
diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be
ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you
plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.

To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA
lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each
folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look, a REQUIREMENTS.md
describing how the PWA works and a TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md describing how it is built.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how this is built, and
[TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how it is checked.

## One app, one setup

Mine installs as **one** app on the phone, with one icon. The apps in the subfolders are pages
inside it, not separate installs.

This is what makes the central requirement work: **the GitHub repo and token are entered once,
in the main app, and every app in a subfolder uses them.** Verified on iPhone and Android.

## Main app

A tile per app: its `icon.svg` above its folder name.

Above the tiles, apps may contribute a summary. The calendar's shows today's entries and the
next one — which matters, because opening the app is the only reminder that works (see below).

## First run

1. Open the app URL and add it to the home screen (iOS: Share → Add to Home Screen;
   Android: menu → Install).
2. The setup screen asks for GitHub owner, data repo, branch, and a personal access token.
3. The app tests the connection and reports clearly if it fails.

Settings are stored on the device only. The token is never displayed again after entry, and the
app warns 14 days before it expires.

Two settings belong to Mine rather than to any one app, and the same two rows appear in the main
settings and in each app's: **theme** (system, light or dark) and **date format** (auto, which
follows the device's locale, or `dd.mm.yyyy`, or `mm/dd/yy`). Both default to following the
device, so Mine looks like the rest of the phone until you say otherwise.

One convention is the same in every app: **a save icon is green and a trashcan is red**, wherever
either appears — a trashcan is red even where it only clears one field of a form that has not
been saved, because the rule is the icon, not the consequence. Both are **glyphs on no
background**: a save is a green disk, a trashcan is a red trashcan. **Nothing in Mine is a filled
green button.** The weight of a primary action comes from the icon being the familiar one in the
familiar place, not from a block of colour — and a save drawn like the rest of the row cannot be
mistaken for a background that means something. The `x` that closes or abandons something is
neither green nor red, and stays plain.

A second convention follows from it: **the `x` is rightmost in every popup**, and the row ends
trashcan, save, `x`. The way out of an overlay is in the same corner wherever you are, so leaving
one is never something to look for — and that corner is worth more to the button reached for by
habit than to the one aimed at deliberately. The save keeps its familiar place beside it, which
is enough, because what makes it findable is the green disk and not the edge of the card.

## Markdown bodies

Every app keeps its text as markdown, so every app has to show it. **One renderer, in `shared/`,
used by all of them** — the calendar's details body today, a zettelkasten note and a diary entry
next. Two renderers would drift, and a note that looked right in one app and wrong in the next
would be the plainest possible sign that these files are not as portable as the whole idea claims.

It is **deliberately small**, and covers what a personal note actually holds: paragraphs, `#` to
`###` headings, bullet and numbered lists, `- [ ]` and `- [x]` checkboxes, **bold**, *italic*,
`code`, and links. No tables, no blockquotes, no fenced code blocks and no images — each of them
is more code to own for something an agenda or a diary page rarely carries, and the app that first
genuinely needs one can add it then.

A checkbox is **rendered, not operated**: `- [x]` draws a ticked box, and ticking it is an edit of
the text like any other. A body is read far more often than its checklist is advanced, and a
tappable box would have to write a file from a screen whose whole point is that it writes nothing.

**It builds nodes, never HTML.** The renderer makes DOM elements and sets text, so nothing in a
body can turn into markup: a body carrying a `<script>` tag shows that tag as text. This is the
threat the CSP exists for — injected script on our own origin — and a data file in your own repo
is the likeliest thing to carry a stray angle bracket. A link is rendered only for `http`, `https`
and `mailto`; anything else stays text, so a `javascript:` URL is never something to press. Links
open in a new tab, because leaving the app would lose the view you were in.

It is hand-written rather than vendored. It is small enough to be, and the dependency table in
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) asks of everything in it what would be
wrong with hand-rolling it — for this, nothing.

## Using it

- Changes appear instantly and are queued for GitHub in the background.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error.
- Offline, the queue is kept and sent when you are back online or reopen the app.
- Editing the same entry on two devices never loses either version: the other device's version
  keeps the file, yours is kept beside it and flagged, and the sync indicator tells you there is
  something to review. Nothing is discarded and nothing is silently overwritten — but the app
  does not interrupt you to ask which to keep, because by then you are somewhere else.
- Everything works offline, including dates and search, because the app keeps a full local copy.

## Reminders

**Mine cannot notify you while it is closed.** No browser can schedule a notification for later;
this is a platform limitation, not a missing feature. Alerts are stored with each entry and
exported, and they fire while the app is open. The summary on the tile screen is the reminder.

## Updates

When a new version is deployed the app shows "Update ready — reload". It never updates while you
are in the middle of editing.

The banner appears only when the version waiting to take over genuinely differs from the one
running. A new worker can sit waiting while being identical to the active one, so "a worker is
waiting" is not the test — if it were, the banner would appear on an app with no update at all
and never go away. Reloading twice with no deploy in between must leave no banner.

## Privacy

Your data lives in a **private** repo. The app itself is public, but it contains no data, and the
token is scoped so that it can only touch the data repo.

them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is a save's green: in all of Mine green is a save and red is
a trashcan, and a green toggle would make a lit flag read as a commit.

### The details body

Last in the popup, and **shown in full and rendered** — not clipped to two lines, not as raw
markdown — by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card
and the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing, and that
is the one thing the old preview existed for, so it is not spent on making the body look like the
rows above it.

It carries a small header of its own: the `lines` icon, and the trashcan at the right when there
is a body to clear. **Clicking the body makes it active**, replacing the rendered text with the
raw markdown in a textarea and putting the trio at its foot. A body is read far more often than
it is written, which is the same argument the rows make, with more text behind it.

### A new entry

A new entry has nothing to read and no file to write to, so it opens **with its title row already
active** and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day preview's `+`, or a
kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well.

**Saving the title creates the entry.** Until then there is nothing to write a field into, so the
other rows are inert and drawn dimmed, and closing the popup writes nothing at all — a `+` opened
and thought better of leaves no file and no commit. Once the title is saved the entry exists and
every row behaves as it does on any other entry.

That is why the title is the row that creates it: an entry must have one, so it is the only field
whose first save can be the file's first save.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **every row saved while
  the popup is open**. It has to be visible and it has to be one choice: asked again at each
  save it would be a prompt on every field, and left implicit it would be the kind of thing that
  silently rewrites a rule. It is set before the row it applies to, which is the order the two
  controls already sit in.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

A row's save **writes the file, closes the row back to text, and leaves the popup open**. The
push runs in the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the row: you stay where you
were, looking at the entry you just changed, which is the whole point of editing in place.

Deleting the entry and skipping an occurrence both close the popup and land on the calendar,
because neither leaves anything to look at.

### Discarding an edit

**The only unsaved work in the popup is what is typed in the active row**, so that is what the
prompt guards. Pressing the row's `x`, pressing the popup's `x`, clicking the backdrop or pressing
Escape, while an active row has been modified, are one way out and ask one question: a small
centred prompt offering **discard** or **keep editing**. An untouched row closes without a word —
the question is about losing work, and there is none to lose. A half-written new entry counts as
work, which here is the same statement: its title row is the row that has been typed into.

The prompt carries a **don't ask again** toggle. Ticking it silences the prompt on that device for
good, so the `x` goes straight back to discarding. That is a preference about this screen's
behaviour rather than data, so it is stored on the device like the rest of them — and it has a
row in the panel's settings section, because nothing in Mine may be switched off from a place
that cannot switch it back on.

raw markdown in a textarea and putting the trio at its foot. A body is read far more often than
it is written, which is the same argument the rows make, with more text behind it.

### A new entry

A new entry has nothing to read and no file to write to, so it opens **with its title row already
active** and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day preview's `+`, or a
kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well.

**Saving the title creates the entry.** Until then there is nothing to write a field into, so the
other rows are inert and drawn dimmed, and closing the popup writes nothing at all — a `+` opened
and thought better of leaves no file and no commit. Once the title is saved the entry exists and
every row behaves as it does on any other entry.

That is why the title is the row that creates it: an entry must have one, so it is the only field
whose first save can be the file's first save.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **every row saved while
  the popup is open**. It has to be visible and it has to be one choice: asked again at each
  save it would be a prompt on every field, and left implicit it would be the kind of thing that
  silently rewrites a rule. It is set before the row it applies to, which is the order the two
  controls already sit in.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

A row's save **writes the file, closes the row back to text, and leaves the popup open**. The
push runs in the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the row: you stay where you
were, looking at the entry you just changed, which is the whole point of editing in place.

Deleting the entry and skipping an occurrence both close the popup and land on the calendar,
because neither leaves anything to look at.

### Discarding an edit

**The only unsaved work in the popup is what is typed in the active row**, so that is what the
prompt guards. Pressing the row's `x`, pressing the popup's `x`, clicking the backdrop or pressing
Escape, while an active row has been modified, are one way out and ask one question: a small
centred prompt offering **discard** or **keep editing**. An untouched row closes without a word —
the question is about losing work, and there is none to lose. A half-written new entry counts as
work, which here is the same statement: its title row is the row that has been typed into.

The prompt carries a **don't ask again** toggle. Ticking it silences the prompt on that device for
good, so the `x` goes straight back to discarding. That is a preference about this screen's
behaviour rather than data, so it is stored on the device like the rest of them — and it has a
row in the panel's settings section, because nothing in Mine may be switched off from a place
that cannot switch it back on.

content.text:
Done. Summary of what the merge changed in the docs:

**`calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md`** — `## Entry popup` and its subsections rewritten:

| | Decision recorded |
|---|---|
| Structure | One popup. Top row = type (marker when it exists, live pair when new), trashcan, `x`. **No pen, no disk** |
| Rows | `icon + value`; unset shows the field's name muted; set rows sort to top |
| Editing | Click a row → editor **inside the row**, right end becomes the canonical **trashcan, save, `x`**; one active row at a time; a row's trashcan doesn't activate the row |
| Saves | A row's save **writes the file and queues the push** — up to four commits for a four-field edit, stated as the accepted price |
| Fields | **Five** rows (category, repeat, alerts, location, participants); **details is the body**, rendered in full at the foot under an icon+trashcan header, clicked to become a textarea |
| Category | A tap on a group **is** the save; its active row has trashcan and `x`, **no save**. Repetition explicitly does *not* commit on dropdown change |
| Title / when | Both are click-to-activate rows; the when reads `MON, 20.11.2026 · 09:00–10:00` and opens the four inputs inline |
| Toggles | Stay one-tap and write through — justified against the board card's `<` `>`, which already does |
| New entry | Title row active on open, other rows inert and dimmed; **saving the title creates the file**; abandoning a `+` writes nothing |
| Repeating | Scope pair + `skip this one` under the title, governing every row saved while open — which reverses the old "the scope pair is not here" rule, and says why |
| Discard | Narrowed to the active row; a saved row is past the prompt's reach; `Confirm discard` row stays, so the panel stays at nine |

**`calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — new `## Writes from the popup` section with the three hazards write-through introduces, plus the module list and the overlay rule (`#sub` now exists only for the group manager; one builder, no `viewCard` beside `fillForm`).

**`TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — the read-only/pen/sub-popup checks replaced with checks for the merged popup, including the ones that must now come out the *opposite* way (the scope pair is present; no pen anywhere) so a copied old assertion can't survive.

Three things I'd flag for implementation:

1. **The stale-occurrence bug is the real risk here.** The popup holds the occurrence it was opened with; after the first row's save that object is a generation behind, and the *second* save goes out against a dead base — landing as a conflict against a file the user just wrote, while the first row still displays correctly. It's documented in both the technical and test docs because it will not look like a bug.
2. **A date save moves the file** (the day is in the path, no rename API), so the popup has to follow the entry to its new path or the next save writes a file that no longer exists.
3. **Queued writes to one path now collide.** Several saves can queue before a drain, and `POST /git/trees` would get the same path more than once. The documented fix is to collapse per path keeping the last text — the `baseOid` needs no choosing, since `putFile` leaves the local `oid` alone on a queued write.

content.text:
Yes — and it's the better trade. Going back to a draft kills all three hazards at once: no stale occurrence (one write, at the end), no mid-edit path move, no queued writes colliding on one path. It also restores "one entry edit is one commit", which the write-through model was spending.

What it costs is the thing write-through bought: the popup no longer always shows what's stored. A row saved and left looks committed when it isn't — which is exactly why "the save button appears only when something changed" matters, so let me pin down what that button is.

**Each row is edited in place, and one save writes.** The rows hold a draft; nothing reaches the
repo until the popup's own disk, so **one entry edit is one commit** and the popup is one
transaction rather than a stream of them. A row that writes the file the moment it is saved was
tried on paper and gives this popup three faults it cannot see: the entry it is holding goes a
generation stale after the first write, a saved date moves the file out from under it, and four
rows saved offline queue four writes to one path. One save at the end has none of them.

**The disk appears only once something differs from the file**, and it is the only button in the
popup that writes. A popup opened to read has no save in it to wonder about — which is most
openings — and a save that is there is a save with something to do.

```
[☑]                                  [trash] [x]      opened, nothing changed
[☑]                          [trash] [disk] [x]       a row has been changed
[☑] [📅]                             [disk] [x]       a new one: the type is still a choice
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry, the disk
once there is something to save, and an `x` to close. On an entry that already exists the type is
a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and
not pressable — because a task turned into an event drops its stage, its importance and its
estimate, and the type is settled when the entry is made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the
event selected.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group: deleting is not an edit of a field, it writes at
once whatever the draft holds, and the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two
taps depends on the trashcan being on the first of them.

Below the row, in this order: the **title**, the **scope and skip** row on a repeating entry, the
**when**, the **toggle row**, the **five field rows**, and the **details body** last.

### A row, and a row being edited

Every row is **the icon, then the value** — no field name beside it:

```
[ball]    Work                                      [trash]
[pin]     Conference room 3B                        [trash]
[repeat]  Repeat
[bell]    Alerts
```

The name is gone because it said the same thing as the icon it sat beside, in the one column
where the value has to fit. **An unset row shows the field's name in its place, muted** — which
is what an empty input does everywhere else in Mine, and what keeps a bell from being a bell and
nothing else. A set row reads as a value; an unset one reads as an invitation.

- **The rows that are set move to the top.** Set fields come first, unset ones follow, and inside
  each group the order is always the canonical one below. Setting a field lifts its row into the
  top group and shuffles nothing else, so a row never moves for a reason you did not cause.
- **A set row carries a trashcan at its right**, which clears that field in the draft. An unset
  row has nothing to clear and carries none.
- **Clicking a row makes it active.** The value becomes the control for it, in the row itself,
  and the row carries **a trashcan and an `x`** — and **no save of its own**. The `x` puts the row
  back as it was, so one field's typing can be abandoned without abandoning the popup; clicking
  another row, or the disk, takes what is in it. There is exactly one save in this popup and it
  is the one in the top row.
- **Only one row is active at a time.** Clicking another row accepts the one that was open.
- **Clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row.** This is the rule a kanban card already
  holds to, and it matters more here, because the trashcan now sits on the surface being tapped.
  The row and its controls are one place where a click that does two things is easy to build.

**Five of the six fields are rows**, in this canonical order:

- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

The sixth, **details**, is not a row: it is the body, and it is drawn in full at the foot of the
popup — described below. A markdown body is the one value that cannot be read on one line, so a
row is the wrong shape for it, and putting it first in the order the way a row would be sorted
pushes everything else below the fold on any entry with an agenda in it. It keeps its place in
the canonical order of fields everywhere that order is a list of fields; it simply is not one of
the rows that order sorts.

**Every editor opens in its own row.** There is no popup over the popup any more: the field
popups are gone, and with them the rule that a sub-popup never writes to the repo — the rows do
not write either, so there is nothing left to carve out. The card scrolls, so a textarea fits in
a row as well as it fitted in a card of its own. The one survivor of that mechanism is the group
manager behind *edit groups*, which is not editing a field.

**Picking a category takes it.** Tapping a group puts it in the draft and closes the row — there
is nothing more to say about a choice from a list, and with no save in the row there is nothing
for a second tap to press. It is the one row that closes itself.

content.content:
### A new entry

A new entry has nothing to read and no file to write to, so it opens **with its title row already
active** and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day preview's `+`, or a
kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well.

**Saving the title creates the entry.** Until then there is nothing to write a field into, so the
other rows are inert and drawn dimmed, and closing the popup writes nothing at all — a `+` opened
and thought better of leaves no file and no commit. Once the title is saved the entry exists and
every row behaves as it does on any other entry.

That is why the title is the row that creates it: an entry must have one, so it is the only field
whose first save can be the file's first save.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry says so under the title, and carries two things the rest do not:

- **the scope pair**, `this occurrence` or `whole series`, which governs **every row saved while
  the popup is open**. It has to be visible and it has to be one choice: asked again at each
  save it would be a prompt on every field, and left implicit it would be the kind of thing that
  silently rewrites a rule. It is set before the row it applies to, which is the order the two
  controls already sit in.
- **`skip this one`**, which drops a single occurrence. That is an action on the entry like
  deleting it, not a change to a field, so it sits with the scope rather than among the rows.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md'
s=open(p).read()
start=s.index('## Writes from the popup')
end=s.index('## Modules')
new = """## Writes from the popup

The popup holds a draft and writes once. The disk is `createEntry` on a new entry, `updateEntry`
on a saved one, and `saveOverride` when the scope pair says `this occurrence` — so **one entry
edit is one commit**, and the occurrence the popup was opened with stays valid for as long as the
popup is open, because nothing has moved under it.

**Per-row write-through was considered and rejected**, and the reasons are worth keeping, because
each of them is invisible until it bites:

- the popup would have to re-point at the saved entry after every write. `S.reload()` rebuilds
  the model, so the occurrence held by the popup is a generation stale the moment a row saves,
  and its `baseOid` with it. The row that saved looks perfectly correct — it put the value there
  itself — and the *next* row's save goes out against a dead base and lands as a conflict against
  a file the user just wrote;
- a date change moves the file, the day being in the path and the API having no rename, so the
  popup would have to follow the entry to a new path mid-edit or write to one that no longer
  exists;
- several saves can queue before a drain, offline or faster than the chain runs, and
  `POST /git/trees` is handed one entry per queued item — so the same path would appear more than
  once in one tree, which the save-once popup cannot produce.

A draft has none of these, and the only thing it gives up is that the popup shows a value the
file does not yet hold. The disk appearing exactly when the two differ is what says so.

**`snapshot(D)` is what the disk and the prompt both read.** It already exists for the discard
prompt: the draft's editable parts, serialised, compared against the baseline taken when the
popup opened. The disk's presence is the same comparison, so there is one definition of *changed*
and not two to drift apart — a disk that shows when the prompt would stay silent, or the reverse,
is that one function having grown a second copy.

Switching the scope pair rebuilds the draft from the other file and **must retake the baseline**.
A baseline left behind reads as changed, which puts a disk in the top row of a popup nobody has
edited and makes every way out ask about changes nobody made.

"""
open(p,'w').write(s[:start]+new+s[end:])
print("ok")

write-through design could not make, and it is the reason for the draft, so it is checked as a
count and not as an outcome.

the field in the draft — the row drops to its muted name and the disk appears — and that it does
**not** write on its own. That **clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row**: the field
is cleared and no input appears, which is the same rule a kanban card holds to and matters more
here, the trashcan now being on the surface being tapped.

`Category Work` — and that the field's name appears **nowhere** in a set row. That an unset row
shows the field's name in its place, in the muted colour and not the plain one, resolved from the
computed colour against the two tokens rather than from a screenshot. That the **five** rows read
category, repeat, alerts, location, participants in that canonical order on a task and on an
event alike, with **details not among them** — it is the body at the foot, and a details row
appearing in the list is the body having been flattened into one; that **every one of the five

while the order inside each group stays canonical.

still empty and the disk is now showing. That the repetition row, by contrast, stays open when
its dropdown changes, because a rule is the dropdown and the ends control together.

and **every other row live** — clicking one opens its editor — with the when seeded from where it
was created, and that a `+` in a kanban column header seeds the stage, read off the toggle row.

disabled state and not from how it looks. That closing it writes **nothing**: no file appears and
the queue is empty, which is what keeps a stray `+` from leaving an `Untitled` behind.

row is inactive — the whole text, not a clipped line — and that clicking it replaces the rendered

event takes all three away again. That stage cycles through three stages in three badge colours

loses its badge once cleared. That a tap on any of the four **changes the draft and not the
repo**: the disk appears, the queue stays empty. That `24h` and `!` light with the ordinary
enabled background and never with `--good`, because green is the disk's, and that nothing else in
the popup lights at all. That the row sits **below** the when row, not above it — resolved from
the elements' document order, since a row that merely looks right can still be the old one.

correctly but was built in the old order cannot pass — and a check that only counted three

switching rebuilds the draft from the other file, so it has to retake the baseline too, and a
baseline left behind is what puts a disk in an untouched popup and makes every way out ask about
changes nobody made.

content.content:
## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so
does every other overlay in the calendar: the hamburger panel and the day preview. Nothing rises
from the bottom edge any more. A centred card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend
to be a drawer that can be dragged.

**There is one popup, and it is both.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day preview, or
as a card on the board — opens the entry, shown as text, and **every value in it is edited where
it is read**: click the thing, change it, save it. There is no pen, no second popup behind one,
and no mode to be in.

It was two before, a read-only preview with a pen into a form, and the reason was sound: a form
answers *what day is this on* in input boxes, which are harder to read than text and leave every
value one slip away from a tap meant to scroll. Editing in place keeps that — a row is text until
it is clicked, so there is still nothing to slip into — and gives back the two things the split
cost. A change was five taps: open, pen, row, field save, entry save. And the preview and the
form had to agree about every field twice over, in two blocks of code, which is how one of them
came to show the stage and the other to hide it.

**Each row is edited in place, and one save writes.** The rows hold a draft; nothing reaches the
repo until the popup's own disk, so **one entry edit is one commit** and the popup is one
transaction rather than a stream of them. A row that writes the file the moment it is saved was
tried on paper and gives this popup three faults it cannot see: the entry it is holding goes a
generation stale after the first write, a saved date moves the file out from under it, and four
rows saved offline queue four writes to one path. One save at the end has none of them.

**The disk appears only once something differs from the file**, and it is the only button in the
popup that writes. A popup opened to read has no save in it to wonder about — which is most
openings — and a save that is there is a save with something to do.

```

once there is something to save, and an `x` to close. On an entry that already exists the type is
a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and

content.text:
Switched to the draft model across all three docs.

**What changed from the write-through version:**

| | Now |
|---|---|
| Saves | **One**, in the top row, and it appears only once something differs from the file. It's the only control that writes |
| A row | Trashcan + `x`, **no save**. The `x` puts that one row back; clicking another row or the disk takes what's in it |
| Toggles | Tap changes the draft, not the repo — the disk appears on the first tap |
| Category | A tap on a group still closes the row in one tap; it just stages instead of writing |
| New entry | A draft like any other edit: every row live, when seeded, **disk disabled until the title has text**. The title-first/inert-rows rule is gone |
| Closing | The popup's `x`, backdrop and Escape prompt discard / keep editing, as today; `Confirm discard` stays, panel stays at nine rows. A row's own `x` never prompts |
| Commits | One entry edit is one commit again |

**`calendar/TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — `## Writes from the popup` rewritten: the draft model, then the three write-through faults kept on record as *considered and rejected*, so the idea doesn't come back without them. Plus two new technical requirements the appearing disk creates:

- **`snapshot(D)` drives both the disk and the prompt.** The function already exists for the discard prompt; the disk's visibility must be the same comparison, or a disk that shows when the prompt stays silent (or the reverse) is that one definition having grown a second copy.
- **Switching the scope pair must retake the baseline.** It rebuilds the draft from the other file, and a stale baseline reads as "changed" — which puts a disk in the top row of a popup nobody edited and makes every exit ask about changes nobody made. This was already a latent bug in the old code; the appearing disk makes it visible.

**`TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md`** — the popup checks now include the ones this model needs and the old one couldn't express:

- The disk appears on a change and **goes away again** when it's undone by hand — that's what catches a flag set on first touch rather than a real comparison.
- **One edit is one commit**, checked as a queue count: four things changed, one write.
- Nothing writes before the disk: the queue stays empty through row saves, toggle taps and a category pick.
- A row's `x` reverts only that row and leaves the rest of the draft alone.
- The prompt and the disk agree in both directions.

One thing worth knowing: the "appearing disk" means the top row's control count changes while the popup is open. The `x`-is-rightmost check reads button positions, so it needs to assert the order both with and without the disk present — otherwise a layout that inserts the disk to the right of the `x` passes whenever nothing has been edited yet.

Record the full-width calendar, the zoom, the hamburger and the one popup

columns instead, or a wide monitor reads a year as ten months and then two.

platforms, so the caret it needed when the label zoomed is gone. The zoom
moved to a button of its own in the filter's slot: day/week/month/year in a
calendar view, vertical/horizontal on the board, where vertical stacks the
three stages and the phone's pager has nothing left to page.

The filter and the settings merged behind one hamburger, filter above
settings. That is what left a slot for the zoom without the phone's first row
gaining a fifth control.

The view popup and the edit popup merged into one. A row is text until it is
clicked, then an editor in the row itself with a trashcan and an x; the pen is
gone, field sub-popups are gone, rows show values rather than field names, and
one disk in the top row appears when something differs from the file and
writes it. Per-row write-through is recorded as rejected, with the three
faults it hides: a stale occurrence after the first write, a date change
moving the file mid-edit, and several queued writes to one path.

calendar view, vertical/horizontal on the board, stored per device under
calendar.boardOrientation. Stacked, the three stages are full width and no
header carries a pager, because nothing is off screen to page to.

The filter moved out of app.js into the panel above the settings, behind one
hamburger. That kept the pane at four controls while the zoom arrived, and it
took the third user off openPop, so the two overlay mechanisms are now the
picker and the zoom.

The view popup and the edit popup are one popup. A row is the icon and the
value, text until it is clicked, then an editor inside the row with a trashcan
and an x and no save of its own; unset rows show the field name muted, set rows
sort to the top and carry a trashcan. The body stays rendered in full at the
foot. One disk in the top row appears when the draft differs from the file -
the same snapshot comparison the discard prompt makes - and writes it. The
field sub-popups are gone; #sub survives for the group manager alone, which
edits no field of an entry.

content.text:
Pushed. Three commits on `main`: the docs, the implementation, and the worker bump.

**What's live:**

- **Full-width calendar, capped board.** `#cal` has no `max-width`; the cap moved to `.view.vK .kb`. The pane is full width in both views, so it doesn't change shape when you switch.
- **Year view** caps at six columns — the formula subtracts the five gaps, because a bare `100%/6` fits only five tracks and reads a year as 5+5+2.
- **Label opens the picker**, every view, both platforms. Caret gone. Desktop gap of ~1rem either side; the phone's `‹ ›` now match the first row's icon size.
- **Zoom** (magnifier) in the filter's old slot: day/week/month/year in a calendar view, vertical/horizontal on the board, current one marked, anchored dropdown. Orientation persists per device; zoom level doesn't.
- **Stacked board** full width with no pagers, drag still works, cards keep their arrows on a phone.
- **Hamburger panel** titled "Calendar": Filter above Settings.
- **One entry popup.** Icon + value rows, muted field names when unset, inline editors, per-row trashcan, no pen, no sub-popups. One disk in the top row that appears when the draft differs from the file.

**352 checks pass** (unit + browser, 320/360px light and dark), and I eyeballed the real app at phone and desktop widths.

Two things to look for when you test, because they're the parts I'd least trust:

1. **Accepting a row's edit.** A row has no save — the value is taken when you click *another* row or the disk, and the row's own `x` reverts it. Type a location, press the row's `x`, and it's gone. That's the agreed design, but it's the thing most likely to feel wrong in the hand.
2. **The time inputs in the when row** render as `04:00 PM` in the headless browser's locale; on your devices they'll follow the phone's. Worth a glance that the row doesn't overflow at 320px with a 24-hour locale.

One thing I did not do: `calendar.boardOrientation` has no row in the settings panel, by the spec we agreed — it's picked in the zoom only.

content.text:
Pushed. The row `x` now closes and keeps, and sits at the top right of the open row next to the trashcan.

**What changed:**

- `closeRow()` no longer reverts — the editor has been writing into the draft since the first keystroke (that's what makes the disk appear), so there was never anything to "accept". The `restore`/`revert` machinery that backed the old behaviour is gone with it.
- The trashcan and `x` moved from under the editor onto the row's first line, beside the field name. This also fixes something I hadn't flagged: under a textarea the `x` landed in a different vertical position on every row depending on the editor's height. The body's header was already this shape, so now every open row matches it.
- Clearing a field is still the trashcan beside the `x`; undoing a whole entry's edit is still the popup's `x`, which is the one that asks.

**355 checks pass**, including three new ones: that the `x` keeps what was typed and still writes nothing, that the pair sits above the editor, and that the `x` is rightmost — the last two read from document order and left edges rather than appearance, so a layout that looks right but was built the old way fails.

Worker bumped to `2026-11-23.3`, so the installed app should offer "Update ready — reload".

One consequence worth knowing when you test: there is now **no way to undo a single field's typing** short of the trashcan (which clears it entirely) or closing the whole popup with the `x` and discarding. That's the direct trade for the `x` not throwing work away, and it's what you asked for — but if typing over an existing value and wanting the old one back turns out to matter, the fix would be the trashcan growing an undo, not the `x` reverting again.
